BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: A brief upper-level ridge will build in the region behind the upper low on Saturday, providing dry conditions until the next strong low pressure system begins to move into the northwest coast late Saturday/early Sunday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Another round of valley rain and mountain snow Wednesday through Friday.
- Winter Weather Advisory issued for northern Harney County OR today until 4 PM PDT.
- Accumulating snow Wednesday morning will impact roads in SE Oregon. Higher southern mountains will see moderate to locally heavy snowfall totals through Friday.
- Long-term pattern remains cool and unsettled this coming weekend through early next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A warm frontal passage will steer upward across our area ahead of an incoming Pacific upper low digging across the northwest and Great Basin through the end of the week. This system will bring a stronger cooling trend, and drive snow levels down to valley floors this morning. Breezy southeasterly winds will also be expected with this system moving in, with gusts 30-40 mph over exposed areas and higher terrain this afternoon. An approaching band of precipitation from the west will bring widespread snowfall over southeast Oregon early morning through late morning today. Lower elevations in eastern Oregon will see up to 2 inches, with 2-5 inches across mountain passes and over higher terrain through Wednesday afternoon, impacting Hwy 20 and 26 north/west of Vale. As such, a Winter Weather Advisory has been issued for this corridor in northern Harney County OR from 4 AM to 4 PM PDT.

Precipitation will spread into SW Idaho later today, returning continuous valley rain and mountain snow through Friday. By the evening today, snow levels are expected to climb back up to the 3500- 4500 ft range, limiting further snow accumulations to higher elevations. The upper low center will steer across our area and the northern Great Basin Thursday through Friday, continuing episodes of precipitation throughout the area. The strong southerly flow on Thursday will slightly increase temperatures and drive snow levels up to the 4000-5500 ft range mainly on the southwest Idaho side. The higher snow levels will result in rain through Thursday evening across most lower elevation valleys including the Snake Plain. It won't be until late Thursday night that a mix or change over to snow will occur as the upper low passes to our east, shifting the upper flow more northerly and allowing colder air to filter in. This cooldown will drop snow levels down to valley floors again, favoring the likelihood of valleys seeing a wintry mix and dusting of snow Friday morning through early afternoon. By late Friday, higher terrain areas in both eastern OR and west-central ID could see total snow accumulations of 3 to 8 inches, with up to 10 inches over high peaks. Precipitation will taper off east come Friday late afternoon/evening as the upper trough pushes out of our area.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A brief upper-level ridge will build in the region behind the upper low on Saturday, providing dry conditions until the next strong low pressure system begins to move into the northwest coast late Saturday/early Sunday. Latest guidance now has the first band of precipitation brought about by this low arriving over eastern OR early Sunday. The precip coverage for Sunday remains weak, with under 30% chances for valleys and up to 50% for mountains. Another brief upper-level ridge will sweep across the area Monday into early Tuesday before another Pacific system moves in and brings widespread precipitation chances yet again for Wednesday. Temperatures will hover near or slightly below normal in SW Idaho and 5-10 degrees below normal in SE Oregon throughout the long term period. Breezy winds will accompany systems passing through.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Guidance throws another weak shortwave towards our forecast area sometime early next week, with generally light QPF amounts over the mountains.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - First wind event of the season for the northern Front Range mountains and foothills this morning. Gusts of 60-75 mph with isolated stronger gusts possible.
- Brief potential for wind gusts of 40-50 mph and isolated stronger wind gusts for wind prone locations near the base of the foothills this morning.
- Elevated to critical fire weather conditions across portions of the foothills, I-25 corridor, and Palmer Divide today.
- Better chances for mountain snow Friday and Saturday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The first part of this storm system arrived earlier this evening as a band of rain and snow progressed from southwest to northeast across the mountains. There was enough moisture to maintain this band of precipitation as far east as the continental divide, with webcams from CDOT and various ski areas showing some brief light to moderate snow... though accumulations were generally around an inch. A few orographic snow showers are expected to continue overnight with minimal additional snowfall totals.

The second part of this system will be the wind. Surface observations across the higher Front Range foothills have been slowly increasing over the last couple of hours, with a few gusts in the 45-50 mph range noted in the last hour or so. Near term guidance has been too bullish with the initial development of the mountain wave, and I would expect that we continue to see a slow increase in wind gusts overnight before the mountain wave begins to become better established closer to 12z. From an ingredients perspective just about everything is "marginal". While the ridgetop/cross-barrier flow is around 45-55kt, the stable layer is somewhat diffuse and a bit higher than you'd expect for a more classic mountain wave. The setup is also rather brief - with the wave quickly diminishing after 18z Wednesday when winds transition to more of a subsident/gradient type regime. Ultimately the current headlines seem representative enough. We still expect a few gusts around 75 mph over the foothills with a few gusts to around 60 mph possible for the typical wind prone areas near the base of the foothills. These winds will also produce some fire weather concerns during the day (discussed further below).

Thursday still looks to be a quiet day across the forecast area as we sit in between systems in a dry southwesterly flow aloft. Forecast high temperatures will be back in the 50s again across most of the plains.

Our next system of interest is still on track to arrive on Friday. Across the plains, Friday looks mild and breezy in a broad southwesterly flow regime. Meanwhile, boundary layer moisture should increase across the higher elevations, and should allow mountain snow showers to develop as early as Friday morning. The first of two shortwaves races across the northern half of the state during the day, and aided by a 110kt jet streak... this could produce a band or two of light to moderate snow accumulations across the central/northern mountains.

The second of two shortwaves associated with the large scale trough then pivots through the region Friday night into Saturday. This should provide another round of snow across most of the higher elevations. There's been noteworthy shifts with the timing/orientation of this wave in relation to the northern stream vort max in this period, and it seems likely there are still several shifts to go here. In the meantime, this interim solution is a bit wetter across the plains, with a handful of deterministic solutions (and about 30-50% of ensemble members) producing some very light snow accumulation across portions of northern Colorado. I would like to see a few more cycles of both physics-based and AI ensemble guidance before getting to enthused about precip chances along the I-25 corridor.

Guidance throws another weak shortwave towards our forecast area sometime early next week, with generally light QPF amounts over the mountains. There's also a good signal that cooler weather will arrive and stick around through at least the first half of next week, with temperatures near/below normal favored.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: This storm system will be driven by a slow moving longwave trough remaining to our north, and several vort-maxes rotating around it between Thursday night and Sunday. This will keep unsettled and chillier weather over the area through the weekend.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - High winds will continue through the afternoon hours today.
- Wind gusts of 60 to 75 mph are expected in the typical wind prone areas along Interstates 80 and 25, with gusts up to 65 mph possible in adjacent zones.
- Strong, gusty winds and a very dry airmass will produce favorable conditions for the rapid spread of wildfire over the High Plains today. Red Flag Warnings are in effect.
- Chances for snow showers return to the mountains Thursday night through Saturday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Strong, gusty winds will remain the primary concern for the next 12 hours or so. GOES water vapor channel imagery this morning shows the axis of a sharply negatively tilted trough pushing into our area this morning. Cloud cover and moisture ahead of the trough axis are moving east of the I-25 corridor at this time, with subsidence and thus stronger winds following shortly behind. Short amplitude mountain wave activity is apparent as local mid-level drying in the lee of the Snowy and Laramie ranges. The high wind forecast is largely on track with strong, gusty winds spreading into most zones so far. Widespread gusts are in the 50 to 65 range, with localized mountain wave activity pushing some areas up to around 75 mph. A few 80+ mph gusts cannot be ruled out this morning. The only change concerning the high wind headlines this morning was upgrading the watch to a High Wind Warning for the Shirley Basin and Laramie Valley (and accelerating the start time) due to the observation of prevalent mountain wave activity. This will allow the stronger winds to creep a bit outside of the typical gap wind areas and into the lee valleys and High Plains. Height and pressure gradients are peaking now, but will hold fairly steady through the early afternoon hours before rapidly weakening mid to late afternoon. Therefore, the winds are seeing now are expected to continue and spread eastward through the early afternoon hours. Outside of the High Wind Warning (far eastern Wyoming and western Nebraska), we should see winds picking up quickly this morning, becoming widespread by 9AM. Look for gusts of 40 to 55 mph in these areas, though a localized gust over 60 mph cannot be ruled out. Once the winds turn westerly, we should see any bits of lingering fog (currently around the Scottsbluff and Alliance areas) clearing out quickly.

In addition to the strong winds, a very dry airmass will be moving in over the area today. Very low dewpoints in the teens to even locally single digits will spread eastward. While temperatures will not be all that warm today, the low dewpoints will still produce RH around 15 to 20% over much of the High Plains. While we probably won't have very widespread conditions actually getting below 15% RH for 3 hours, the wind conditions and critically dry fuels are reminiscent of several significant wind events from last season which created fire control issues despite RH above critical. Therefore, decided to upgrade the Fire Weather Watches to Red Flag Warnings, as conditions will certainly be favorable for the rapid spread of wildfire.

Winds should die down quickly this evening for most locations, though the mountains and wind prone areas may remain breezy for a few more hours. With a cooler airmass in place, most locations should drop into the 20s to start off our Thursday. Transient ridging will try to build in over the area on Thursday, but it won't have much time to boost temperatures. Highs should be near or slightly above seasonal norms, generally in the low to mid 50s across the area. Winds will be lighter Thursday, but still breezy to locally windy in Carbon county. The wind direction will be SSW west of I-25 and SSE east of I-25. The extremely dry airmass that settles in today will be gradually eroded from both the west and east tomorrow, but locations in the vicinity of the Laramie Range (Albany, Platte, and Laramie Counties) can expect to see very low RH Thursday. Fortunately, winds should be below critical, but fire weather conditions will be elevated in these areas.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The next Pacific trough will approach the area Thursday night. This system has trended towards a slow-moving, disorganized open wave with generally good agreement amongst ensemble members. Saturated southwest flow will push into Carbon County Thursday evening, initiating another round of snow shower activity for the mountains. The primary lifting mechanism will be orographic, but models actually show a decent amount of convective instability west of the Laramie Range Thursday night and Friday. So, accumulation is most likely where the southwest orographic lift is most favorable (the Sierra Madre Range), but we will need to watch for locally heavy snow shower activity, potentially even bordering on snow squall criteria, spreading out of the mountains. Snowfall rates could be high at times due to the instability, but coverage is expected to be spotty outside of the mountains. The higher peaks are favored to see accumulating snow, with a 80+% chance for Advisory criteria amounts in the Sierra Madre range, and a 40% chance in the Snowy Range. Thursday night and Friday, precipitation is expected to be confined to areas along and west of the Laramie Range. The surface cold front will be slow to move into the area, which should allow much of the High Plains to see another mild day Friday, even while Carbon, Albany, and Converse counties turn colder. Once the surface front pushes in from the northwest, sometime Friday late afternoon or evening, we will see north to northwest winds at the surface, which will be more favorable orographic lift for the High Plains. Snow falling east of the Laramie Range Friday night into Saturday morning is still the less likely solution, but probable enough to warrant a mention.

This storm system will be driven by a slow moving longwave trough remaining to our north, and several vort-maxes rotating around it between Thursday night and Sunday. This will keep unsettled and chillier weather over the area through the weekend. Look for highs below seasonal averages, breezy conditions, and possibly a few snow showers though expectations for QPF are limited. The flow aloft will transition to a more zonal pattern by early next week. However, models are in pretty good agreement keeping a chilly high pressure system over the northern plains pushed up against the mountains, which should keep temperatures on the chilly side for several more days. The overall weather pattern should remain active with additional Pacific troughs moving inland over the area, but almost all ensemble members continue to bring these storms through on an unfavorable track, limiting snowfall chances.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Cold air in the wake of this system will keep afternoon highs below normal through the extended forecast, with morning lows below freezing. The latest freeze on record for Grand Junction's Walker Field sits at November 26th.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Rain and snow will taper across the mountains early Wednesday morning. Motorists can expect slick roads on mountain passes.
- Winds will taper some overnight, but remain gusty into the morning hours of Wednesday as this system exits.
- Temperatures will trend downward late week, with colder air delivering the first freezing temperatures for some desert valleys.
- Another storm will bring measurable snowfall to the mountains Friday and Saturday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Rain and snow showers will continue to work across the Divide early Wednesday morning, as the storm system lifts out onto the Plains. Mountain passes will remain slippery overnight, but drier conditions and clearing skies will improve road conditions by mid day Wednesday. Clouds will begin to clear out in the afternoon and temperatures will only recovery slightly as we remain a few degrees below normal. Winds will remain gusty against the Divide through the morning, then lighten from southwest to northeast as the upper level winds subside.

A brief transitory ridge moves overhead Thursday, pushing temperatures back up a few degrees. Unfortunately, clouds will begin to invade again, ahead of a low diving out of the PACNW into the Great Basin. Winds will begin to pick up again across the Four Corners on Thursday, as a strong jet streak rounds the base of the low digging into the Great Basin. By Thursday afternoon, the Uncompahgre and San Juans will see gusty winds too. Thursday evening, another plume of moisture will work into northeast UT and northwest CO, with rain and snow showers developing. Snow levels drop into the 6-7k neighborhood Thursday night and continue to lower Friday, with most of the CWA below freezing by Saturday morning. Mountain snow will pick up in the Uintas Thursday night and spread southeast across the CO mountains through Saturday morning. A few low valleys might see a dusting by Saturday morning, should cold air hold with this system. Otherwise, it looks like some of the best snow will favor the central mountains of Colorado. This forecast could vary as the track of the low adjusts, but for now it looks like a broad swath of 6-8 inches of mountain snow and locally higher totals on favorable aspects.

Cold air in the wake of this system will keep afternoon highs below normal through the extended forecast, with morning lows below freezing. The latest freeze on record for Grand Junction's Walker Field sits at November 26th. In an anomalously warm and wet fall, it looks like this record will live on another year thanks to the arrival of cold air in the valley with this storm. High pressure moves across the region late this weekend and starts off Thanksgiving week. Models are hinting at another disturbance crossing the region Tuesday, with perhaps, the beginnings of another unsettled period for the holiday weekend. More on that to come in subsequent forecast packages.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Temperatures will remain cool through early next week with another fast moving upper trough moving through Monday or Tuesday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Gusty winds behind a departing system will bring brief elevated fire weather conditions across portions of El Paso, Teller, Fremont and northern Pueblo Counties, though fuels are only critical across El Paso county.
- Snow ending across the mountains early this morning with another round of light accumulations Thursday Night/Friday along the Continental Divide.
- More strong wind and rain and snow showers possible for Saturday with a low chance of showers across the southeast plains Saturday, though any precipitation looks light.
- Cool down for the weekend through early next week with another system possible Monday or Tuesday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Progressive upper trough crossing the mountains and glancing by to the NW has spread snow across the Continental Divide into the Sangre De Cristos overnight. Winds have been gusting up to 60 mph or a little greater at times across the higher mountains and spotty areas along the eastern slopes. Drier air has been working into western areas on the back side of the system early this morning, which will bring a rapid end in snow showers towards dawn.

We will see an increase in winds along the lee of the southeast mountains towards 09z when downward forcing maximizes behind the trough axis, but winds aloft will increase quickly resulting in strong forward shear towards 12z which should limit any mountain wave activity to very localized areas at best. Some brief gusts to 50 to 60 mph will be possible along the eastern slopes of the southeast mountains. Otherwise, dew points will drop behind the system late this morning, setting the stage for localized elevated fire weather conditions in the afternoon across portions of El Paso, Teller, western Pueblo and eastern Fremont counties. Fuels are only deemed critical across El Paso county and winds will be decreasing in the afternoon as humidity values fall below critical thresholds. Therefore, elevated fire weather conditions looks too brief and limited in coverage for Fire Weather Highlights at this time. Temperatures will remain mild today in spite of some cooling aloft as deep mixing offsets this some. Didn't stray far from NBM high temperatures.

Tonight will be clear and cold, especially across some of our mountain valley locations where efficient radiational cooling will result in teens and some upper single digit lows. Temperatures across the plains will range from the upper 20s to around 30.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The active weather pattern continues with increasing southwest flow on Thursday ahead of the next western U.S. upper low advancing eastward towards the Great Basin. Snow spreads into the southwest mountains and Continental Divide Thursday night through Friday as energy ejecting from the mean upper trough glances by to the northwest. Main upper trough ejects eastward across CO on Saturday, though the system is pretty fast moving and open, suggesting colder temperatures and some brief rain/snow showers behind the frontal passage Friday night/Saturday. Snow amounts across the mountains look light at this point, as the system appears to lack a persistent deep moisture tap. But the snow will be wind driven with the potential for 2-6 inches across the Eastern San Juan mountains through early Saturday morning where orographics will be maximized. The central mountains will see considerably less given the less favorable orographic component. And the southeast mountains and plains will see a brief chance for showers but given the open and progressive nature of the system, any amounts look localized and brief unless the upper circulation can intensify a bit more and pull winds to a more northeasterly upslope component. NBM shows the odds of snow amounts greater than an inch at less than 25% across the southeast mountains and Palmer Divide, so odds of measurable snow is not looking good at this point. Will have to watch the potential for some strong winds on Friday with the latest data suggesting gusts up to 50 to 60 mph will be possible.

Temperatures will remain cool through early next week with another fast moving upper trough moving through Monday or Tuesday. It doesn't look like a big precipitation maker at this point, but more light snow for the Continental Divide looks probable along with cooler than normal temperatures for the plains.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: With colder air spreading into the region late this week, freezing temperatures will be possible around the St George and Zion Canyon areas Friday and Saturday nights.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Another storm system will bring significant mountain snow Thursday into Friday, with snow levels falling near to below 5000 feet by Friday. Another 6 to 12 inches of mountain snow, with locally higher amounts near 2 feet for the upper Cottonwoods is expected in northern Utah, while 4 to 10 inches of mountain snow is forecast for central and southern Utah.
- Freezing temperatures are increasing in probability for the Virgin River corridor near Zion National Park Saturday and Sunday mornings.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: An energetic, negatively tilted shortwave trough continues to lift through northern Utah/far southwest Wyoming this evening. While the better forcing is shifting north and east of the forecast area, orographically enhanced snowfall will persist across northern Utah through the remainder of the evening before diminishing overnight. Thus far any enhancement from the GSL has been minimal, however the potential remains as -10C 700mb temperatures remain over the area. Large scale subsidence in the wake of the ejecting trough will bring and end to any lingering precipitation overnight, and have adjusted the going Winter Wx Advisories to end at 4am across the north, while canceling the remaining advisory for southern Utah.

Shortwave ridging will bring a temporary drying trend Wednesday as a cool and more stable airmass settles across the forecast area. Max temperatures will remain in the 40s across most northern/western valleys Wednesday afternoon, running roughly 5 degrees below climo.

The next upper trough to impact the region will make landfall along the Pacific Coast on Wednesday, then gradually spread inland and cross the Great Basin/Intermountain Region during the Thursday/Friday timeframe. Unlike the current trough, this late- week system will come through in a more piecemeal fashion. The initial surge of moisture advection will arrive Thursday, however this plume will be cresting the Sierra which will block a substantial amount of moisture from penetrating further inland. A portion of this upper trough is forecast to eject across the region Thursday night into early Friday, followed by the larger scale trough axis Friday night into early Saturday. As such, widespread heavy precipitation looks unlikely during this timeframe, but when all is said and done the northern mountains are looking at another 6-12" (locally higher) with a half inch of QPF in the valleys. Colder air with the main trough axis Friday will lower snow levels to the valley floors of northern Utah with some accumulation possible, particularly along the benches. Precipitation across southern Utah will remain largely focused on the Thurday-Thursday night window, thus lower precip totals are expected.

With colder air spreading into the region late this week, freezing temperatures will be possible around the St George and Zion Canyon areas Friday and Saturday nights. On the topic of freezing temperatures, KSLC fell to 32 degrees this evening, which tied the date of the latest first fall freeze on record (2021 and 2016).

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: Avalanche danger at higher elavtions will rise on Wednesday as new snow and increasing wind will deposit wind-drifted snow onto a weak snow surface. You'll find this recent wind-loading near and above treeline on slopes facing west through north to east.
Below treeline the conditions are generally safe due to thin or non-existent snow cover.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe and lack sufficient coverage for an avalanche. At high elevations, steer clear of isolated patches of firm, drifted snow below ridges or in steep gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has begun to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. 6-12 inches of new snow has fallen between Friday the 13th and Monday the 16th. Another 6-12 inches could stack up by the end of the week. If you're traveling in the mountains this week, watch out for wind slabs 1-2 feet thick above 7,000 feet and pay attention to terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: From 60-degree temperatures to over a foot of new snow, the weather sure has changed quickly over the past week. A cooler and wetter weather pattern has taken shape over our region since Friday the 13th. As of Monday (16th) afternoon, some mountain locations have picked up 6-12 inches of new snow along with southerly winds gusting 20-30 MPH.
Wind Slabs
• Wind slabs could become reactive this week with over a foot of new snow and gusty winds. Wind slabs will be most sensitive just below ridgelines.
• Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices.
• Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
• Strong winds and local terrain features can alter the prevailing wind direction. Pay attention to cross-loading and wind-loading on unsuspecting slopes.
Early Season Conditions
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.
Check Your Winter Gear

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
Continuing Education
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with the winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
Observations
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

bottom_line: Increasing winds and new snow will raise the likelihood of encountering pockets of stiffer, wind-blown snow at higher elevations. These isolated wind drifts could produce small avalanches.
